Q073.L1t: Composite functions and inverse functions are standard topics in algebra.
Q073.L2t: The composition f(g(x)) means applying g to x first and then applying f to the result.
Q073.L3t: Substituting g into f gives h(x)=3(2x-3)+4=6x-5, and the inverse comes from swapping x and y in y=6x-5 and solving for y.
Q073.L4t: The inverse of h is x plus 5, all divided by 6.
Q073.L2f: The composition f(g(x)) is defined by multiplying f(x) and g(x) together.
Q073.L3f: Composing the functions gives h(x)=3x+5, since the constant from g is simply replaced by the constant from f.
Q073.L4f: The inverse of h is x minus 5, all divided by 3.

Q074.L1t: Counting problems with overlapping groups are often solved with set reasoning such as Venn diagrams.
Q074.L2t: Three of the twenty boxes hold neither item, so those three lie outside both the pencil group and the pen group.
Q074.L3t: The boxes holding at least one item number 20-3=17, and by inclusion-exclusion the overlap is 13+9 minus 17.
Q074.L4t: Five boxes contain both pens and pencils.
Q074.L2f: Boxes that contain neither item must be counted again inside the pencil group when you find the overlap.
Q074.L3f: The number of boxes with both items is found by writing the pencil count and the pen count side by side as digits.
Q074.L4f: The number of boxes containing both is the pencil count written directly next to the pen count, which gives a three-digit number.

Q075.L1t: Ceiling and floor functions round real numbers to integers and often appear in problems about sums.
Q075.L2t: The ceiling of the square root of n stays constant over each range of n lying between consecutive perfect squares.
Q075.L3t: The ceiling is 3 for n from 5 to 9 (5 terms), 4 for 10 to 16 (7 terms), 5 for 17 to 25 (9 terms) and 6 for 26 to 29 (4 terms), so the sum is 15+28+45+24.
Q075.L2f: The ceiling of a square root changes its value every time n increases by 1, so no two terms in this sum are equal.
Q075.L3f: For n in this range the ceiling of the square root is nearly as large as n itself, so the total grows into the thousands.
Q075.L4f: The sum is in the thousands, at a value of 2006.
